$comment: The guide's narration for Albert Einstein, rewritten to sound like a museum guide (owner decision 2026-10-17). Each line keeps its source cue and fact ids. 'source' is the approved chapter sentence (content/einstein/chapters/<n>.json, itself checked against the verified claim); 'text' is the caption and what is spoken, 'speak' (optional) only spells out an abbreviation for the voice. Only pronouns, connectives and word order may differ from 'source': assets-src/audio/check_narration.py fails if a content word, date, place or number of the source is missing or a new one is added (names may become pronouns after the first mention; connectives are listed there). Audio: build_guide_audio.py, one clip per line per guide voice. A chapter keyed by its kind (birth, leaving, ...; app/src/tour/data/chapters.js) carries that chapter's opening line (spec 2.5, owner feedback round 8: a human sentence, not a dateline: what happened, where and when, one human detail, an invitation to look around): 'source' lists the verbatim claims of its 'fact_ids', and check_narration.py allows no date, number, place or content word they lack beyond a short invitation list. Voice key '<slug>:ch:<kind>:opening'.

lines.source: Nine letters were written by Albert Einstein to Lieutenant Stephen Brunauer of the Research and Development Division. Albert Einstein's letters to Lieutenant Stephen Brunauer relate to Einstein's research with the Research and Development Division of the Navy, specifically underwater explosions and a proposed electromagnetic torpedo detonator.
lines.text: Nine letters were written by him to Lieutenant Stephen Brunauer, of the Research and Development Division, and the letters relate to his research with the Research and Development Division of the Navy, specifically underwater explosions and a proposed electromagnetic torpedo detonator.

lines.source: Albert Einstein's letter of June 18, 1943 to Lieutenant Stephen Brunauer discusses Albert Einstein's idea of an electro-magnetic device that will automatically explode a torpedo as it passes underneath a ship.

lines.source: In a letter of July 30, 1943, Albert Einstein reveals that he has come up with a mathematical simplification to analyze the impact an underwater explosion would have on the hull of an armored ship.
